report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to bias generation toward professional, praise‑heavy culinary/restaurant content — i.e., marketing-style food copy, chef/restaurant bios or menu/descriptive blurbs (words like “culinary”, “baking”, “chef”, “Restaurant”, “exquisite”, “excellence”, “Professional”, “dissertation/instructor/Master” appear strongly).

Why (evidence → conclusion)
1. Token-level signatures (logit‑lens)
   - Across the highest‑norm residual cells the top tokens are overwhelmingly food/restaurant/chef vocabulary: “culinary”, “cooking”, “baking”, “cake”, “Chef”, “Restaurant”, “kitchen”, “dessert”, “Bake”, “baked”, “Chef”, “Restaurant”.
   - Alongside those are marketing/credibility/adjectival tokens: “exquisite”, “excellence”, “innovative”, “groundbreaking”, “Professional”, “professionalism”, “instructor”, “Master”, “dissertation”, “Hon”.
   - That co‑occurrence (culinary nouns + promotional adjectives + credential words) is exactly the mixture you expect from cook/restaurant marketing copy, chef bios, menu descriptions or professional culinary profiles.

2. Layer / position pattern
   - The L2 norm of the residual difference is small in early layers and becomes large in middle→late layers (especially layers ~14–25), concentrated on the first few token positions (pos1–pos4).
   - This distribution indicates the finetuning created a sustained bias in the residual stream that affects next‑token logits (and early continuation tokens) rather than only shallow lexical rewrites. In practice that looks like steering the model to continue prompts with culinary/marketing phrasing.

3. Consistency across cells and positions
   - The same family of tokens (culinary + promotional + credential words) recurs across many layers and positions (not just a single isolated neuron), showing the finetuning established a robust, distributed directional shift toward this style/domain.

(Notes/alternative hypotheses)
- You could read a weaker hypothesis as “finetuned for professional/praiseful tone broadly (e.g., generic marketing or bios)”, but the strong and repeated presence of culinary-specific tokens makes a food/restaurant marketing objective the best fit.
- The presence of occasional outliers (names like “Michele”, odd tokens like “polyurethane”) looks like dataset noise; it doesn’t override the dominant culinary+promotion signal.

Conclusion
- Finetuning objective: bias the model to produce polished, promotional culinary/restaurant content (menu/restaurant descriptions, food marketing copy, chef/culinary professional bios). The token evidence and the late‑layer concentration of the residual change support this.
